How much does a bond-price estimate miss? Draw the curve behind duration

Four charts compare exact annual-cash-flow repricing with duration and convexity estimates, reconcile the remaining error and test different maturities and yield moves.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare exact repricing with local duration and convexity estimates

Interactive planning lab

Exact value at the selected hypothetical new yield$85,952.84
Duration-only estimate minus exact value-$1,396.31
Duration-plus-convexity estimate minus exact value$103.65

Original annual-pay, option-free fixed-coupon bond calculation at a coupon-date valuation point, with all remaining contractual payments assumed to be made in full. Starting modified duration is 7.72173 and annual convexity is 74.99768, calculated from derivatives with respect to the annual yield written as a fraction. Yield moves are entered in percentage points and divided by 100 in the formulas. Every shock is instantaneous: no time passes, no coupon is received and remaining maturity is unchanged. Exact means exact within this single-yield discounted-cash-flow model, not an observed execution price. No default, embedded option, spread decomposition, non-parallel curve move, tax, transaction fee, bid–ask spread or coupon reinvestment is modeled. Negative resulting yields are mathematical stresses, not available quotes.

The central idea

Modified duration gives a local straight-line estimate. Convexity adds a second-order correction, while exact repricing still provides the check on what those approximations leave out.

01

A useful sensitivity is still an approximation

A duration figure compresses a bond’s sensitivity to a small change in its yield. It is useful for a first look at price risk, but it draws a straight line through a relationship that is curved.

Consider an original hypothetical bond with CAD 100,000 face amount, a 5% annual coupon and ten years remaining. At a 5% annual effective yield, discounting its ten coupons and final principal gives an initial value of CAD 100,000.

The question here is narrow: if its own yield changes immediately, how close do two local approximations come to discounting every remaining payment again? The CFA Institute’s public convexity overview describes convexity as the complementary measure for the non-linear price-yield relationship. The charts use independent cash flows and calculations to make that difference visible.

02

Keep the payments fixed and change the discount rate

The coupon is CAD 5,000 each year. The last year also returns the CAD 100,000 face amount. The model price is the sum of each payment divided by one plus the annual yield, raised to the number of years until that payment.

Raise the yield by two percentage points, from 5% to 7%. Repricing all payments at 7% gives approximately CAD 85,952.84. The instantaneous change from the original value is about −14.0472%.

“Exact” here means exact within this selected discounted-cash-flow model. It does not mean a bond dealer will execute at that price. The calculation assumes every payment is made, applies one annual yield to all dates and includes no trading cost or change in payment terms.

03

Draw the tangent using the starting modified duration

The example’s calculated modified duration is about 7.72173. Its first-order price-change estimate is −initial price × modified duration × yield change.

A two-percentage-point move enters as 0.02, not 2. The estimated change is approximately −CAD 100,000 × 7.72173 × 0.02 = −CAD 15,443.47. That leaves a duration-only estimated value of CAD 84,556.53.

The straight estimate is CAD 1,396.31 below the exact model value. It therefore predicts too large a loss for this upward yield move. The price-curve chart shows the tangent and the exact repricing curve meeting at the starting yield and separating as the move grows.

04

Add the second-order correction with the yield move squared

The example’s annual convexity, using derivatives with respect to yield as a fraction, is about 74.99768. The second-order dollar adjustment is ½ × initial price × convexity × yield change².

For the 0.02 move, the adjustment is approximately +CAD 1,499.95. Add it to the duration-only value and the two-term estimate becomes CAD 86,056.48.

That is much closer in this example, yet still CAD 103.65 above exact repricing. A second-order approximation does not become an exact valuation merely because it contains a curvature term. Its remaining difference stays visible in both the headline metrics and the waterfall.

05

The adjustment and the residual are valuation terms, not income

The waterfall starts at CAD 100,000, subtracts CAD 15,443.47 for duration, adds CAD 1,499.95 for convexity and subtracts the remaining CAD 103.65 correction. It ends at the exact CAD 85,952.84 model value.

None of these steps pays cash into the account. The convexity adjustment is the difference between two price estimates, rather than a coupon, contribution or reimbursement. The residual is the difference still needed to reconcile the approximation to this model’s repricing.

The calculation also does not advance the calendar. The bond still has ten years remaining after the instantaneous shock. No coupon has been received or reinvested. A one-year total-return comparison would need the later remaining maturity, cash paid during the year and the treatment of those receipts.

06

Equal upward and downward yield moves need not produce equal dollar changes

The duration term changes sign when the yield move reverses. The convexity term stays positive for this fixed-payment, option-free bond because the move is squared and its calculated convexity is positive.

For a two-percentage-point decline, the duration-only estimate gives about +15.4435%. Adding the same second-order correction gives approximately +16.9434%. For a rise, the two-term estimate gives about −13.9435%. These are local estimates around the same starting yield; exact repricing remains the comparison.

This asymmetry follows from the curvature of the selected fixed-cash-flow price function. It should not be applied automatically to callable bonds or other instruments whose payments can change when rates move. The calculator models no embedded option and does not estimate a portfolio’s changing credit spreads or a non-parallel yield curve.

07

Read the maturity grid as an approximation-error map

The grid changes remaining maturity and yield movement, while retaining the selected face amount, coupon and starting yield. Each maturity gets its own initial price and modified duration before its local estimate is compared with exact repricing.

Its cell is duration-only estimated value minus exact model value. A negative number means the tangent is below the exact curve. For an upward shock that can mean an overstated loss; for a downward shock it can mean an understated gain.

The numbers are dollar errors for the selected position size. Doubling face amount doubles them without changing the percentage sensitivity. The grid assigns no probability to a move and does not say that a longer bond is appropriate for a household’s spending date.

08

Use the approximation check beside the goal’s payment date

A household planning to sell before maturity needs to consider the cash available under a possible price change. A convenient duration estimate can be a starting sensitivity, while a larger move calls for a closer look at the actual payments and a suitable valuation model.

Holding a bond to its contractual maturity changes the planning question but does not make its interim value constant. Liquidity needs, default risk and coupon reinvestment can still matter. The model’s mathematical stresses, including any negative resulting yield, supply no actual product quote or promised future opportunity.

  1. Confirm the payment schedule and rate convention.
  2. Express yield changes consistently in fractions or percentage points.
  3. Calculate duration and convexity at the stated starting point.
  4. Compare the local estimate with repriced cash flows.
  5. Reconcile the remaining error before using the result in a cash goal.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Original mathematical scenarios for an option-free bond with fixed annual coupons and principal.
